texts: bad: the cargo phrase 'with twelve full buckets of salt-bloom' is slotted as the instrument of the returning — i.e. the means by which the party travelled — which asserts a manner your sentence never states; a 'with'-phrase has only two licensed readings, an animate co-participant or the means, and carried cargo is neither, so the buckets are either mis-slotted or have to be dropped. Give the carrying its own finite verb: 'On day 34 of Year 1, the harvest party returned to Cauldron Hall at dawn and carried twelve full buckets of salt-bloom.' Everything else lands well — the date, dawn, Cauldron Hall as the destination, the count of twelve, 'full' distributed to each bucket, and the salt-bloom held in the buckets.
good. a plain copular clause: the harvest is typed and the past tense wraps the 'heavy' atom, which is exactly the licensed shape — nothing extra is reified and nothing is invented.

good. 'into the store' is read as the destination of the pouring with no invented result state, the salt-bloom reuses the symbol introduced in sentence 1, and the compound 'salt-bloom store' keeps its 'store' genus.

mixed: the universal is handled well — one fireable per-compartment rule ranging over the store's compartments, with the 'each' recorded alongside it — but 'with the date' lands in the instrument slot, so the date reads as the tool the labelling was done with rather than as the content written on each compartment; there is no licensed slot for inscribed content, so that is a near-fit rather than a faithful record. If the date matters as content, put it in the object position: 'Hesper wrote the date on each compartment of the store.'

good. 'stayed potent' takes the continuation shape exactly — the potency reified with a 'still' marker and past tense, plus the flat property atom so a plain 'is it potent?' still resolves — and the salt-bloom keeps the symbol it was given in sentence 1.
